utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Belinda Pidwell, Joanna Korner, Nathanael Burris, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, David O'Brien, and Mark Iaconelli for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we start, I would like just to address the Trial Chamber on two issues, and I will speak in Serbian in order to be fully and properly understood. [Interpretation] Your Honours, following the instructions issued by the Trial Chamber requesting us to take a position by Friday, this week, with regard to the Prosecution request to introduce General Mladic's journal into evidence in this case, we would like to inform the Chamber that today we are going to submit our joint motion. That is the joint motion of the two Defence teams of Stanisic -- teams of Stanisic and Zupljanin. What I would like to say at this point which is not mentioned in our motion is that, at this juncture, the Defence challenges the authenticity of the journal. I do allow for a possibility, Your Honours, that our position regarding this can be altered but only once we have received the complete set of documents from the Prosecution. Since, at this point, we, indeed, have only a few written documents, plus the documents that were submitted and disclosed of late, whereas, the entire video and audio material has still not been disclosed to us by the Prosecution and we know that that has been done in some other cases. Therefore, once we have received this material we shall be able to give our exact position concerning this issue. This is all I wanted to explain to the Trial Chamber. The second issue, Your Honours, relates to the testimony of Mrs. Ewa Tabeau. Of course, you are aware that the Defence has expressed their position with regard to her testimony in our motion dated the 31st of August, 2009. Then, in March of this year, 2010, we received an additional report to which we also objected. There's no ruling concerning on these two motion yet; but, nevertheless, I would like just to briefly express the views of the Defence team of Mr. Stanisic pertaining to this matter. The summary pursuant to 65 ter relating to witness Mrs. Tabeau submitted along with the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution quotes that Mrs. Tabeau is a demographic expert that was going to testify about the internally displaced persons and refugees in the territory of 47 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina of which some are relevant for this particular indictment. Our position, Your Honours, is that Mrs. Tabeau's report, both in the Milosevic and the Krajisnik cases, was by and large not helpful for the Trial Chamber, nor to the parties in the proceedings either, because Mrs. Tabeau was unable to provide responses to some of the key issues. However, despite this position of ours, we agree, in principle, that a demographic expert can discuss issues relating to displaced persons and refugees in view of her specialised expertise. What has arisen as a problem at this point is her supplementary report, in which Mrs. Tabeau is dealing with the victims of war. That's the report disclosed to us in March of this year. However, she speaks about the victims and divides them into the civilian and military victims, that is to say, the people who were killed. That means that Mrs. Tabeau has been tackling now an entirely new topic for which I personally believe that she doesn't have the required qualification and expertise. Secondly, this topic that she is dealing with now had not been announced to us pursuant to 65 ter as an issue that was going to be testified on by this witness, which is completely contrary to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Besides, this report on the victims of war is based, as much as I could gather, on certain databases which are of dubious credibility, or at least any information about this kind of organisations or databases are something that is totally unknown to us. Just as an example. She makes reference to the data provided by some associations of Muslims against genocide. Then she refers to the data relating to the consensus of household in free territories in the city of Sarajevo in 1994. And, finally, she refers to a document entitled "The Book of the Missing," from 1998. Your Honours, in this case, we still haven't raised the issue, although we discussed it once a few months ago, of forensics and the -- the mechanisms of causing death of the victims, time of their death and other questions that have to be established in a clear and solid manner. We are dealing here with a criminal procedure, and it is quite clear and everybody knows what the Prosecution must prove in any such proceedings. Our position is that on the basis of the supplementary report, for which Mrs. Tabeau does not have the required qualification and expertise the Prosecution is trying to overcome the problem of proving what is essential in every criminal trial. In addition to that, I have to say, that the supplementary report of Mrs. Tabeau is so difficult for me to understand that I absolutely cannot grasp a large number of sentences, neither in my mother tongue nor in English. I do concede that this is my personal problem and probably due to my low IQ. But, at any rate, I believe, Your Honours, that, at this point, the Defence will not be in the position before the Trial Chamber decides whether this supplementary report can be added to the expert report of Mrs. Tabeau as well as of her testimony. I think that it is inappropriate to call Mrs. Tabeau to testify in-chief because, at least as far as the Stanisic Defence team is concerned, we must say that we are not able to follow this testimony in an appropriate way. I am sorry for being so long. I thought I could have spent less time on this, but this is basically what I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Is there a response from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I'm just waiting to see if Mr. Krgovic wants to add anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we support whatever Mr. Zecevic says, because this is the joint position of the two Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At least Mr. Krgovic didn't say his IQ couldn't follow what Mr. Zecevic was saying. Your Honours, firstly can I deal with the question of the Mladic diaries. Sorry, notebooks properly. Your Honours, we would, therefore, in the light of the Defence indication, although it is somewhat unfortunate that they still haven't really made up their minds as to whether they want to contest the authenticity or not, we would simply ask, as we did in the motion, that we be allowed to add the two witnesses to our 65 ter witness list and we will either tender them under 92 bis or call them hopefully under 92 ter. But that's the situation. As regards the other material, Your Honours, we utterly fail to see how can this can affect the Defences' position toward the authenticity of the notebooks. The other material which we do not propose to use, I hear Mr. Zecevic saying that they're still waiting for disclosure, I think that is probably right. There may have been limited disclosure in some other cases where the matter is perhaps more urgent. But the material, the videos, the SIM cards and the like was being forensically dealt with and that's why there's been the delay in disclosure. They've also got to be downloaded, so it's quite a lengthy procedure. But as I say, we are not proposing -- there's a list being provided to the Defence and to Your Honours with Ms. Gallagher's statement of what the material consists of. We are not proposing to put it in. And so, Your Honours, we would simply ask that Your Honours deal now -- I don't know what the motion is that the Defence are filing because they have already responded to our motion to add and indeed I believe Your Honours were going to rule. We would ask Your Honours merely to make a ruling. Firstly can we add the diaries and the excerpts therefrom to our 65 ter exhibit list, that's not to say admitted into evidence, and can we also add the witnesses. And that's all I think we can say on Mladic. Now, as regards Ms. Tabeau, Your Honours clearly ruled last week. You said she was an expert and you said that both reports could be used for the purpose of her testimony. Mr. Zecevic spent most of the time going behind or attempting to go behind Your Honours ruling, asking effectively Your Honours to reconsider the matter. And, Your Honours, we would say that you have considered the matter carefully over a number of months, have ruled, and therefore Ms. Tabeau is to be treated as an expert and her reports are admissible. The final matter he comes to is that, well, if he is wrong on asking you to reconsider, in any event we shouldn't be allowed to call her tomorrow because he doesn't understand her evidence. Well, Your Honours, that's the whole point of Ms. Tabeau being called. She is going to explain in, we anticipate, simple terms that even someone with Mr. Zecevic's IQ can understand what that evidence is about and how it will assist the Trial Chamber. We have clearly said we do not expect there to be cross-examination. The Defence will have ample time to consider her evidence and to consider their cross-examination with or without the assistance of their own expert. But, Your Honours, we do say she -- the Defence have been notified for some time now that she was going to testify in-chief tomorrow. We have been not using the court time properly over the last few weeks for a number of reasons, one is the inability to get the witness here who was supposed to come the week that we had to have off. The fact that Defence cross-examination estimates have been somewhat overestimates of how long they were going to take, so we had insufficient witnesses here. We say, particularly in the light of the information we received from the Senior Legal Officer yesterday of the estimated length of this trial now, that we should use the time when we can in court. As I say, she is expecting to give evidence tomorrow in-chief and we should be allowed to call her. So, Your Honour, that's the application that we make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, to the extent that I understand -- dealing with the witness, the expert witness, the -- as Ms. Korner has responded, have you forgotten, for want of a better word, that the decision was that she would only be examined in-chief tomorrow and that you have the -- that cross-examination has been deferred. Doesn't that answer the concerns that you have expressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't forgot, Your Honours, of course. But the -- what I -- what I was trying to brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber and the Judges is that -- that we still believe that it would be very hard for us to follow her direct examination on the basis of the documents which have been disclosed to us. I know that -- I know that -- that Ms. Korner and the -- and you, yourself, have the -- have decided on this, and Ms. Korner's argument is valid, I must say. But, still, I just wanted to raise this as an observation with the -- with the Trial Chamber that -- which is creating a relatively big problem for the Defence. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber doesn't intend to make any further comments at this point. It would return to this later in the day, after we would have had a chance to discuss it during a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the Prosecution is ready with its witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There are a couple of preliminary matters in regard this witness which perhaps I can deal with first before he is brought in. The first one, Your Honours, is that he previously testified in 2001 with protective measures of a pseudonym and voice -- facial distortion. He has now -- and those protective measures were confirmed in these proceedings last year. However, upon arrival at the Tribunal, he has asked for those protective measures to be rescinded and now wants to testify openly, so I'm making that application now so that -- so that he can testify in open court. I think a ruling has to be made to overturn the protective measures previously granted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose we should hear from him before we purport to rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The second matter is, this morning the witness handed me a document which he brought with him from the region. It's a -- it's a certificate from the Red Cross showing his release from Trnopolje camp in August 1992. It hasn't been processed through our evidence unit because it was only handed to me about half an hour ago. I have shown it to the Defence and we're having copies made, but I would be seeking to add it to our 65 ter list and use it. I don't believe there will be an objection from the Defence because it's a procedural matter and they will be provided copies as soon as we are able to get them to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So noted, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the third matter, Your Honours, is the allocated time for this witness is 20 minutes. Given that he has now chosen to testify openly and the fact that he has -- it's been ten years or nine years since he testified previously, I would ask that -- for some leniency and to be given a few extra minutes, perhaps 40 minutes in total. We have some photographs to show him and some matters to clarify from his previous testimony. I anticipate it will be approximately half an hour but I'm asking for 40 minutes to be overly cautious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I understand your application for further time. I don't understand how this has anything to do with the manner in which he is now testifying. But there may be a connection which is lost on me. At the -- we will begin and see where we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have a short summary as well of his prior testimony, which I would ask to -- to read out. It's very short. But I can do it now or I can do it after the witness comes in. I'm in your hands in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we, logically, must go into closed session, in order to deal with the mode of testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When you entered the chamber, you were invited to make the solemn declaration and the first thing I must do is to alert you that the effect of that is that you are exposed to the penalties which this Chamber is empowered to impose for perjury should your testimony be inaccurate or incomplete. Could you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mensur Islamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 20th of August, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a BA in law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And did you practice as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What -- what -- what work did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mostly worked in the economy in iron ore mines. I was employed there as a lawyer, later on as a secretary of one part of the organisation, and now I work in the forestry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you would have testified previously before this Tribunal, and therefore, I need only remind you as to the pattern that the -- is followed in terms of the examination of witnesses. The side calling you begins - in this case, the Prosecution - and after that, the Defence would have an opportunity to cross-examine. And the Prosecution could then re-examine you in the -- on matters arising out of what has come in cross-examination. And the Chamber may at the end of that or, indeed, at any point during the -- the examination of counsel themselves have questions of you. The Prosecution has requested a little more than 20 minutes for their examination of you, and counsel for the first accused, Mr. Stanisic, has indicated that they would be an hour; and counsel for Mr. Zupljanin has indicated that their cross-examination would last for three hours. The ordinary times of sitting of the Court are intended to -- in addition to the comfort of the witness, to facilitate the changing of the tapes which are used to record the proceedings, and sessions do not exceed 90 minutes in length. Today, for certain other reasons, we sit at slightly irregular times and we will taking a break at 12.25 in your testimony. And the -- then there will be an hour's break between 1.45 and 2.45 and we expect to rise for the day at 4.00. If, for any reason, you are in distress or otherwise need a break other -- at times other than when the Court would ordinary rise, if will indicate that to us, we would, of course, accommodate you. And I would now invite Ms. Pidwell to begin her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Islamovic, before I start ask you some questions, I'm just going to read out a short summary of the testimony you provided in a previous case because that evidence will not be heard in court today.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness is the first witness you are hearing from the municipality of Prijedor. He has testified once before here in the Keraterm case, Prosecutor versus Sikirica, Dosen and Kolundzija, in 2001. These men were camp commanders and guards of the Keraterm detention facility. Mr. Islamovic lived in the Puharska section of Prijedor, and in May 1992 he saw his elder brother being arrested. He himself was arrested some two weeks later, on the 12th of June, by soldiers and a policeman that he recognised. He, together with another brother, was taken to the police station in Prijedor. He was not interrogated there himself. He was forced to wait outside while his brother was interrogated in the police building and then they were both taken to the Keraterm detention camp in a police van. He spent 55 days at Keraterm. He has testified previously about the location and the layout of the Keraterm camp and the terrible conditions and beatings that occurred there. He described the frequent callouts at night when guards would select a number of detainees and beat them, sometimes to death. He was an eye-witness to the murder of one camp inmate by the camp commander Sikirica, and was in room 1 when a massacre of the detainees in room 3 occurred. He heard the events of that night in July 1992 when a large number of men, possibly up to 200, were shot by soldiers who were let into the camp by the reserve policeman who was the shift commander on duty. The witness saw the clean-up the next day which was conducted under the authority of a different shift commander, another reserve policeman. There were more killings that evening. The witness remained in Keraterm until he was transferred, together with the other inmates, to Trnopolje camp in August 1992 and he was released from there a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Islamovic, do you recall testifying in the case against Dusko Sikirica, Damir Dosen and Dragan Kolundzija, in this Tribunal, on the 22nd of March and the 26th of March, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And have you listened to that testimony you gave, the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, since your arrival in The Hague this week?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again that you were asked during the course of that testimony, would your evidence be the same again today?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I completely stand by the statement and the testimony which I gave to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, as you know, I don't need to ask you questions that you were asked previously in your testimony because you have listened to it and confirmed its accuracy, so I will just take a few minutes to ask you additional questions at this juncture. In -- in late 1991, you were employed at one of the iron ore mines in Prijedor. What was your role there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed as a secretary of the OUR, as part of the organisation iron ore mines Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And approximately how many employees worked at the mine?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Around 5.000 employees were employed at this mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What was the -- the ethnicity of the employees of the mine, generally?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately I think that the ethnic makeup of the employees, the Muslims and the Serbs, was such that their numbers were almost identical. And the number of Croats was significantly lower. They may have accounted for about 10 to 15 per cent of employees, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And can you please explain how it came about that you stopped working there in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: As early as in late 1991 and early 1992, there was an unwritten rule at the mine, that is to say, in the organisation which employed me and also in the municipality of Prijedor in general, that all the employees who had not reported themselves to the army or the reserve police forces were not welcome to the company.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And how was it made known to you that you were not welcome at the company?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: We were officially sacked in May. All the Muslims and the Croats who were fired from work, who, in inverted commas, were disloyal, received written decisions. That meant that these people did not want to go to war in Croatia, that is to say, they didn't want to put on uniforms, were deemed as people undesirable to come to work in that organisation. To put it simply, the guards at the gate refused entrance to those employees who were not wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you, at that time, a member of an armed force? Were you asked to -- were you -- did you receive a call-up?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you involved in any operations to -- to guard your area of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you a member of a political party at that time?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a couple of questions about the day your older brother was arrested on the 31st of May, 1992. You said in your prior testimony that you were able to see him being taken away, as he lived in a house not far from yours. Could you tell the Tribunal who it was that took him away and describe that, please.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: From the window of my house, I was able to see my eldest brother being taken away. Actually, an hour before that took place, I was personally warned by some of my friends living across Puharska, to the effect that the army was surrounding this particular neighbourhood and that from the direction of Cejreci, they were carrying out a mopping-up operation towards the city. I was told not to try to escape because opposite my house there was a railway track and the army took up positions behind the railway tracks. For that reason, they told me not to try to escape because I would probably be shot dead. Only for a moment, and occasionally, I peeked through the window while my brother was being taken away by one soldier carrying a rifle; whereas, the other soldier started the car that was in the garage and drove away. Since my brother and I had two attached houses, they probably did not come to my part of the house, thinking that this must have been one and the same household.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you personally recognise any of the -- the men who were taking your brother away?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the time. Only later I learned from my brother and some other inmates the identity of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When did you next see your brother?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: The only group of inmates from Keraterm that, after seven days and following interrogation at Keraterm, was released, that group, including my brother, consisted of some 15 to 20 detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What did you do from the time your brother was arrested until the time you were arrested, some 12 days later?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: During that time, I and the other brother of mine were in hiding. We didn't dare to venture out. I may have tried to get to the city on two occasions at the most, just to see what was happening and why my brother was taken away. I wanted to see what the situation in the town was. As I said, we went out very seldom and, for the most time, we remained in hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So how did it come about that you were then arrested on the 12th of June?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we couldn't stay indoors all the time. We had to go out of the house, and a neighbour of mine, the second house from me, could not -- said he could not keep looking at us. And then some 12 days later, about -- a number of policemen came, surrounded our house, and arrested my brother and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What was the occupation of this neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, there is a -- some missing in translation. Can you ask witness to repeat the answer who arrest him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, it appears that the interpreters didn't catch your full answer last time. Can you please repeat. My question was how did it come about that you were arrested on the 12th of June. Could you repeat your answer to that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: At around 1500 hours, after lunch, my brother knocked on my door, in my part of the house, and asked me to come out. I didn't understand what this was all about. When I opened the door, I saw about 10 to 12 policemen and soldiers who had come to arrest me and my brother. Among those soldiers and policemen was the neighbour that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What -- what was the occupation of this neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, he was an active-duty police officer. But I think that on the eve of the war, he was pensioned off, but then he was reactivated and engaged as a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall what uniform he was wearing on this day?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: He wore the blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was that a camouflage uniform or a regular uniform?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think it was a camouflage uniform. It was the regular uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You said you saw about 10 to 12 -- sorry, 10 to 15, sorry, policemen and soldiers who came to arrest you and your brother. Were you able to decipher who was in charge of this group?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. But I think that this neighbour of mine, the policeman, was in charge. Because judging by his demeanour, from the moment we were arrested until we were taken to the police station, I concluded that he was the man in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And of the 10 to 15 policemen and soldiers, are you able to tell the Tribunal which were policemen -- or how many police and how many were soldiers, or guess the proportion?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you a decisive answer. Because, really, at that point and later on, that was something the least relevant to me. But let's say, in percentage, that there was equal number of policemen and officers -- and police officers, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was your house searched on that day?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A number of policemen and soldiers entered my part of the house and the brother's part of the house. After they had conducted the search, it turns out that they found nothing because there was nothing to find. And after that, they drove us to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you were taken to the police station, who was driving the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a van, a civilian van, windowless, kind of a heavy goods van that had no windows in the rear. But while we were being driven, the back doors were open. I cannot remember exactly who was in the driving seat. I really -- I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You said in your prior testimony, sir, that your brother was taken into the police building but you were made to wait outside. Do you know why you were not taken inside the building at that time?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't clear to me at the time why that was the case. When we were brought there, we all had to kneel and lean three fingers against the building of the MUP. There was a total of four of us who were arrested. They were taken upstairs, but while I was kneeling there, a police officer approached me from behind and asked me my name. When I told him my name, he said, Get up. Whether that was because, at the time, I spoke to him, I really don't know. So the other three men were interrogated but I, myself, was not interrogated at the police station at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm going ask to you look at a photograph now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3419.44. It's in tab 1. Is it possible to have it a little bigger? That's better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I wonder -- you have the pen, I see. I wonder if you can mark on there the police building with the letter 1 -- the letter A.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recognise the court, the court-house? And if you do, mark it with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if you see your place of work on that photograph, could you mark it with the letter C.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the administration building of my company.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now we see some cars parked right up close to the police building. Can you perhaps indicate with an arrow where your -- the van that you were travelling in came in and parked on the day of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if could you mark the arrow with the letter D, please.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, this photograph was only taken last year. Were there any changes to the -- the building or the surrounds that you have noticed since your detention there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that next to the court-house, between the MUP building and these garages here, there used to be a high metal fence. So when this vehicle driving us came in, all of that was from the front of the MUP. However, this is the back entrance to the MUP where our van was parked and where the garages were, and this is where this high metal fence was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's where you've drawn the line next to the letter D; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I put it a little bit bolder.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And perhaps just to clarify for the record, you mentioned some garages. If you could mark those with the letter E.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: The length of the garages is identical to that of the MUP building, so I would mark it in this way. So these are the garages I'm talking about. The garages -- or, rather, the premises where also people were being interrogated before they were taken to Keraterm or Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were waiting outside the building while your brother was inside, are you able to indicate on the map - if there's room - where you were?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If you could mark on the photograph where you were waiting outside the MUP building while your brother was inside.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Next to the very entrance to the building. That is where we were. Leaning against the wall, next to the door, the main door.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, for the record, the witness has marked a small red dot -- just one moment. Your Honours, it appears that the markings have not been saved. We're going to have to do it again. Perhaps I can lead him through this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, the markings that you so kindly provided to us on the photograph were not saved through a technical problem and we're go to have to go through the process again. Perhaps I can lead you through it. Could you mark with the letter A, the MUP building, please.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And B is the court-house; C is your work.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you mark with the letter D where you were travelling when you came in the van on the day of your arrest. There was an arrow and the letter D.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And E were the garages.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You've marked the fence. And lastly, the red dot where you were waiting outside the MUP building for your brother.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I seek to tender that as an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1520, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, we know from your prior testimony that you were then driven to Keraterm camp. Do you recall the driver of the vehicle that transported you there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him quite well. He was a policeman. If necessary, I can tell you his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Strika. A big man with moustache, a strong man. He was driving the police van.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you see him on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I personally saw him when he brought inmates in, in his vehicle. And I also heard from other inmates that his main task was to bring in Muslims and Croats to Keraterm and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, I can't believe that we're at the point for the break already. So if this is a convenient point, we would break now and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us, upon your arrival at Keraterm camp, who the camp commander was?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that at the time the commander of the camp was Knezevic. Zivko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And had you known this man before your arrival at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that before the war, he was the police commander in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did he remain the police commander during your detention at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think that he was very soon replaced by Dusko Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And was -- did he remain as the commander during the entire period of your detention, or was he also replaced?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: He was also replaced, I think just before the end, and that an elderly man came to his position, but I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: In your testimony, you described the uniforms of the guards as being SNB colour uniforms. Could you please give an actual description of what they were.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Not all the guards who had the olive-drab uniforms had uniform uniforms. Some were from the JNA, and they were solid. Others wore camouflage, that is to say, multi-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say "multi-coloured," is that multi-coloured green or multi-coloured blue?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: As you asked me about the soldiers, they wore the green and beige multi-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were there any other uniforms worn by other guards?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The policemen wore dark blue and light blue uniforms. These were the police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I want to show you a document now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's tab 5, Your Honours. It's 65 ter 463. It has already been tendered as an exhibit, as P662.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you will see that document is headed: "List of police employees to be given special access passes to the Keraterm reception centre." There's a list of some 54 names. It's a one-page document in the B/C/S but it goes to two pages in the English. Just looking perhaps at the first 20 names in the B/C/S, do you recognise any of the names as being people that you saw guarding or in a command position at Keraterm while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zivko Knezevic, as I already said. At the beginning, he was the commander of the camp. Then Dusko Sikirica, who is under number 4, replaced him after that. Tomo Prodan was one of the shift leaders or he used to replace one of the shift leaders. Predrag Banovic was also there, as well as Dragan Coric, numbers 16 and 17. They were guards. I know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2 of the English, please, which are numbers 21 through 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If you look at numbers 21 through 46, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we could pull up the B/C/S a little bit. And do the same exercise.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Number 21, Dusan Fustar, he was one of the shift leaders. Number 23, Lazo Gavrilovic, a guard. Damir Dosen, a shift leader. Drasko Dosen, a guard. Milan Pilipovic, another guard. Dragan Kolundzija, shift leader. Zurnic, a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of the English, please, and just the bottom of the document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slobodan Gnjatic, a guard. Goran Grujic, a guard. Vukasin Vujcic, also a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm going to ask you now look at another aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3419.45. That's tab 2 for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise any of the buildings in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We can see here the building of the Keraterm camp. That was the former Keraterm factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Would you mark the building perhaps slightly above it with the letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you indicate on the map [sic] where the vehicle came in that dropped you off for the first time at Keraterm, which direction it came on the road and where it stopped. Perhaps with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It came from the direction of the town. It was here. Then it turned here. This is where the gate was. And then it passed through here to the reception office, which was just next to the industrial scales. And then it passed to somewhere about here, in front of -- in front of the dormitories, 1 and 2. This is where we got out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you mark the gate with the letter B, please.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And we know that Keraterm had four rooms where people were detained. Could you perhaps show on the rooftop of the building the layout of the rooms, and mark them with 1, 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I have marked immediately -- I have placed the numbers immediately above the doors that led into the particular dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I seek to tender that as an exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I ask the -- does that mean that only a portion of the building was dedicated for use as a camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Behind the numbers that I marked was a section that was not used as a detention facility for inmates, and also the part of the building that is to the extreme right. So this part, let me mark them with a B and a C. So approximately it's just this section which I marked with 1, 2, 3, and 4. That was the part of the building that was used to detain the inmates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered the second question I was about to ask as well. Thank you, sir. Yes, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd like to show you one last photograph. It's in tab 3, 65 ter 3419.46. Sir, if you are able to look at this photograph and mark on it where the MUP building is, if you can see. And mark it with a letter A.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It's a bit more difficult because it's small, but you can recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. And I know you can't see the Keraterm facility on that map, but can you indicate whereabouts it is in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: All the way to the right. So from the direction of Bosanski Novi; that is to say, from my house towards Keraterm and Banja Luka. That's the road and this is the direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the distance between -- the approximate distance between the MUP building and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's approximately a kilometre and a half, or 2 kilometres, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I seek to tender that as an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, you had asked for a little leeway in terms of time. I would point out to you that you have now spent 48 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I only have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, from your prior testimony, we know that you were interrogated during your detention at Keraterm. Do you recall how long after your arrival at the detention facility that interrogation took place?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 20 days to about one month after I initially arrived to the camp, that was the time when I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what were the nature of the questions?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a farce. It was a circus and not an interrogation. They were mainly interested in learning what my brother and I had been doing, whether we had been politically active, whether we were members of the SDA party, whether we had obtained any weapons and so on. Something that made no sense, as far as I was concerned, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were detained there by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, never. But I did suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And how did it come about, sir, that you were later transferred to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Around the 1st of August, there were some unusual activities going on at the Keraterm camp. They used to count us more often or place us into groups and make lists, all kinds of things. In any case, I learned from the guards that the camp would be dismantled and that we would be transferred to Trnopolje. Some people would be sent to Omarska; some to Trnopolje; and some inmates would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How were you transported to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: In buses. The army and the police escorted us, and we were transported there in civilian buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How many days did you spend in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Between the 4th and the 7th of August. Then a friend of mine came there and signed that he would guarantee for me, and that was when I was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: This morning, sir, you handed me a document which you'll now see transformed onto your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: In Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Tribunal what this document is.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. That is the certificate which I received from the municipal Red Cross organisation of Prijedor at the Trnopolje camp. It reads that I arrived there on the 4th of August. And page 2 includes the name of the friend of mine who guaranteed for me, as well as the date when I was released. That was the 7th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: This is the document I mentioned at the beginning of his testimony which he handed me this morning, Your Honours, and a copy has been given to the Defence. I would seek your leave to add it to our 65 ter list and exhibit it at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. We understand the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1524, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not in e-court yet, but we will --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It should be MFI'd because -- pending translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Therefore, Exhibit P1524, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Today on page 15 you said - and let me quote - that you completely stand by your statement and the testimony before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I fully stand by everything that I stated before this Tribunal. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned statements, you meant the three statements which you gave to the investigators of this Tribunal; correct? Did you have that in mind?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Statements stated before this Court are one thing. This is what the Prosecutor asked me. And the statements which I gave to the OTP before my testimony in court are another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this. We have your testimony in the case in which you testified, and there is no doubt about that, because you already accepted that and it's already a part of the package, as we informally call it here, in accordance with Rule 92 ter. That is one thing. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Another thing are the statements which you gave before you came to testify in 2000 and 2001, and you gave them to the investigators of this court.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I apologise, let me clarify. We have to make a digression here. The first statement from 2000, which I gave at the MUP in Sanski Most, is very short. It was given ad hoc, and it is very imprecise. The statement which I gave to the investigators of ICTY was given over the period of three days. It is much clearer, and it could happen that certain details given in the statement to the Prosecutor's office in Sanski Most are somewhat different to the details from the other statement, which is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you, that this is normal, that the statements are not identical, and that a context in which they are given and the time should be taken into account. But the essence of what I understood is that you stand by what you said in the statements and you basically repeated that in your testimony before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: 99.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I read the transcript as the witness being asked have you listened to -- do you recall testifying in the case against Sikirica with three dates. Have you listened to that testimony? And if you were asked the same questions and so on and so forth. So it's -- if I understand it well, the answer was not about all the statements, was about this testimony. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, page 15, line 8 and 9, the question is: "If you were asked the same questions again that you were asked during the course of that testimony, would your evidence be the same again today?" "I completely stand by the statement and the testimony which I gave to this Tribunal." That is the basis of my cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, but that's not -- that's not a question and that's not the answer. Well, you go ahead. You understand it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I will read to you -- I do not wish to tender your statements. I will just read to you a part of your statement to see if you remember that part and whether you stand by that. It is your statement given on the 24th of August, 2001, to an investigator of this court. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: The 24th, the 25th, and the 26th of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. On page 3 of that statement you said the following: "Serb began to arrest people who were of Bosniak and Croatian ethnicity around the 20th of May, 1992. The collection centres were the places where these people were taken and where they were detained for just a few days. The collection centres, between the 20th of May 1992, were operational for about ten days. All the arrested men, women, children and elderly people were brought to these collection centres. The women, children and elderly would be sent to the Trnopolje camp after a day or two. Other prisoners spent three to five days, on average, in these centres. As for per cents, about 95 of those arrested were Bosniaks or Muslims and 5 per cent were Croats. All the people imprisoned in the collection centres were civilians. "These centres were mainly run by members of the Serbian army. However, in each of the collection centres, several policemen were present as well. I have to note that the majority of the staff were the local Serbs who wore military uniforms. In the first two days, no food or water was distributed. If anybody stayed for more than two days at a collection centre, he would be given a piece of bread and a little water." Do you remember that you stated that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely and fully stay by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 16 of your testimony today, answering to a question of my learned friend, you talked about mobilisation in late 1991. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said -- you noted a fact or provided an explanation by saying that beginning in late 1998 [as interpreted] the guards at the entrance of the mine where you were employed did not wish to allow employees who were not wearing uniforms to come and work, if I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the unwritten rule was that all people who were not wearing military or police uniforms were undesirable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 36, line 15, I said towards the end of 1991 not 1998 as the record shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood you correctly, you worked at the mine as the secretary of an OUR.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's one part of that work organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since we understand each other but for the benefit of the interpreters, please let's make pause between questions and answers so that everything can be translated. Sir, you, as part of the management of that company, were not expected to come to work in uniform, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The employees who worked in the mine itself did -- did they have certain equipment, but first let me ask you whether it was an open-pit mine or a --

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was an open-pit mine. And extracted from there was ore -- iron ore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, at any rate, the people working in the mine have to have certain safety equipment, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Proper working clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how these working clothes looked like in the mine where you worked.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I first have to explain the following. You put it rightly when you said that I was part of the management team. Unlike workers who were working in the pit, we were dressed in civilian clothes, in nice clothes, as usual. That applied to people working in the administration, unlike those who were working in pits or in the factory who wore working clothes; that is to say, for as long as the mine and the factory was in operation. But already at the beginning of 2002 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, this is the year that witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I think that nobody at that time thought about the work process. The only thing that everybody thought about was war, and I would like to emphasise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said 2002. I suppose that you meant 1992.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I was talking about early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So, if the employees working in the management section and in the administration service came to work in their normal clothes appropriate for the job that they carried out, and the workers who were working in pits were coming in proper clothes and carrying equipment required for their jobs, I don't understand how come that you ascertained that those who were not dressed in uniforms were denied access to the premises, to the workplace. Did you mean that figuratively, or did you mean it as a fact?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: It is very simple. All the mine employees who were subject to work obligation had to wear uniforms. For the most part, and I can give you some percentages, that involved over 90 per cent of the Serb employees who already in the -- early 1992 came to work, unlike the Muslims and the Croats who did not have uniforms and who, at the time, already were not coming to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I will drop this subject because it is not too important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just one little question. Mr. Witness, does that -- do you mean to say that the Serbs did come in uniform? The 90 per cent of the Serbs, you say, did they come in uniform to the workplace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said, and we need to clarify this for the Trial Chamber, you said that they came because they had work obligation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A number of them was probably subject to work obligation. As for the others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia mobilisation, once it is declared, was carried out in such a manner that it was mandatory for those who were called up to respond; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And those who failed to respond were even accused of committing a criminal offence by doing so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this criminal offence was stipulated by the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Those who were not called up to join military units were called up to perform work obligation, which, essentially, was equal to mobilisation. The only difference was that, instead of carry fire-arms and taking part in military operations, they were working in production and in the industrial sector.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That should have been the case, but it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you theoretically and what the law said?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes that's what the law said. But the fact was that neither I nor my brothers ever received any military or -- or mobilisation summons, either for the military service or for the war -- work obligation. And that apply to the majority of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are aware that mobilisation and work obligation were something that was publicly announced; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Once mobilisation is publicly declared, then the summons are not served personally but that meant that all those falling into this category were obliged to report to the unit according to their assignment. And you also had an assignment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, although you knew that mobilisation was publicly declared, neither you nor your brothers reported to your units.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And that also meant the majority, the vast majority of Croats or Muslims because tacitly nobody accused us of that because we were undesirables. When you said that according to the criminal law sanctions were stipulated for such violations, but we never suffered such sanctions. I assume that that was the case because already at that time they knew how we would end up. We were simply persona non grata at our workplace, but probably we were desired as inmates in camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is a fact, isn't it, that the Party of Democratic Action and its president, Izetbegovic, on several occasions during 1991, called upon the Muslims, the Bosniaks, not to respond to the publicly declared mobilisation by the Yugoslav People's Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it is true that you, members of the Muslim community, Bosniaks, and that applied to Croats as well, did not wish to respond to the mobilisation. That is the truth. It is not true that it was the JNA who did not wish to have you among their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: But I can explain that to you from my point of view. When the Muslims and the Croats saw towards the end of 1991, when they were mobilised and they went to fight in Pakrac and other places there, and when they saw what was being done there, then they themselves, in addition to this appeal that you mention coming from Sarajevo to Prijedor, they themselves decided not to go to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is, isn't it, that such a huge number of Muslims and Croats refused mobilisation in 1991 and that it was practically impossible to have all these people prosecuted; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That could not have been the reason for what happened to us afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony on page 879 and 880 of 21st of March, 2001, while you gave evidence in the Keraterm case, you confirmed that from the window of your house you were watching your brother being taken away on the 31st of May; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, when asked who took him away, you said that it was done by the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, on that same page, you described an event when you and your other brother, on the 12th of June at around 3.00 p.m., if I remember correctly, were taken away; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is what you said: "When I opened the door, I saw some 10 to 12 soldiers with their rifles pointed at me. I was confused. The only one I recognised was a neighbour of mine who was a reserve policeman and he also had his rifle pointed at me. I asked him, 'What is this? What is this all about?'" Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During cross-examination conducted by my learned friend Petrovic on the 26th of March, 2001, on page 968 of the transcript, he asked you the name of the neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he [as interpreted] said that his name was Brane Bosnjak?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But that was the neighbour who had a house that was not next to mine but the second next to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 42 I said that you said that his name was Brane Bosnjak. And this is just for record.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And he was a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then my learned friend asked you about his ethnicity. You said, "I think that he was a Serb." And then he asked you about this armed group, to which military structure they belonged, whether they were police, army, White Eagles, paramilitary, et cetera, to which you responded that all of them were soldiers or at least one could say that based on their uniforms. After they had taken us to the MUP building, I suppose that those were regular JNA soldiers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It is a fact, sir, isn't it, that this neighbour of yours named Brane Bosnjak, and I think you said the same thing today as well, retired sometime before the war.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so. Yes, but before that, he was an active-duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, he worked as an active-duty policeman before the war, then he retired. And when you saw him in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, he was reactivated as a policeman again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, actually, you don't know that, that he was reactivated as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Look, at that point and even in my statement, I said that it was totally irrelevant to me and that I cannot remember all those 12 soldiers, how many among them were actually policemen, how many were soldiers. But for him, I know for sure that he had a police uniform on. As for the others, I don't remember. Whether I was terrified or there was some other reason, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I read a portion of your statement given in 2001, which is nearly ten years ago. You also testified here in another case that all of them were soldiers, judging by their uniforms, and that Brane Bosnjak was a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, when you reach a convenient point, we would take the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one question, and we can -- and I will move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I am reiterating that you don't know for sure whether Mr. Bosnjak was indeed a reserve police officer or if he was perhaps mobilised for Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I know definitely that he was a reserve police officer because he was the only one dressed in blue police officer -- police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can -- we can have a break at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we rise, to resume in an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, can I revert to the matter of Ms. Tabeau which I raised this morning and what I'm about to say may obviate the need for you to make any decision. Ms. Tabeau has been going through, obviously, her tables in preparation for giving evidence. In particular in the victims of war report, although the main body and her main tables will remain completely unaffected and indeed her conclusions, in re-checking -- and I apologise for the fact that the re-checking wasn't done earlier but, in fact, because she has always been a stand-by witness and was away, she only started this week. She has noticed there are some figures in the tables in the annex, annexes, to had report, which need slight correction. It involves, however, five different tables, as I understand it. It does not affect the tables in her main report and the main part of the report nor her conclusions. However, it's clear, I had hoped that the corrections, I was told about this just before the break, would be -- could be done very quickly simply and only affected one table. I'm told it's five. So therefore, really, in order to get it to the Defence but the end of this afternoon even though it doesn't affect, as I say, her testimony, that's not possible. So the -- there are two possible courses. One is that we don't call her at all. Alternatively we call her tomorrow without the corrections to the tables in her annexes. And certainly her report, her original report is wholly unaffected. It has got nothing to do with that. It's only her new one, and she can deal with that. So, Your Honours, to that extent we're in Your Honours' hands and obviously what the Defence feel about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, of course, one of the factors is when would the present -- when the witness who is at present on the stand, when would his testimony be completed. But dealing specifically with Ms. Tabeau, the -- what the Chamber would have been reminding counsel, particularly Mr. Zecevic who would have raised this this morning, is that, in addition to what we had already said about reminding him about her cross-examination being deferred, was the fact that, as is the practice that we have adopted, the application that the -- the -- the Chamber defers its decision on the application to tender the relevant reports until after cross-examination is completed. So the tidying up, for want of a better expression, which you have indicated would occur, would, I suppose, underline the desirability of deferring the admission into evidence of the accompanying material in any event. But we'll see where we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's -- that's -- I -- I take that point in entirely. As I say, Ms. Tabeau can explain when she gives evidence why she wants to alter those tables slightly. So in that event, Your Honours, we're happy for her to start evidence tomorrow. There's only one thing. She's going to be adjourned without cross-examination and, of course, we therefore can't speak to her. But it may well be that we do need to speak to her about the corrections even while she's giving evidence, so that is the only thing we'd ask for leave. Otherwise she'll be, as I say, part heard, as it is giving evidence, so that we can't talk to her normally. That's the only problem that arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The -- in addition to inviting your response on the present question, it may also be useful, while you and especially Mr. Krgovic who had indicated three hours with -- with the present witness, to indicate when we are likely to be finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I indicated one hour, and I believe I used some 35, 40 minutes and I have additional 15 minutes, so I will stick to one hour, what I -- what I anticipated for the cross-examination of this witness. As regards to Ms. Ewa Tabeau, I understand the position -- we take no position on this application. We stated -- I stated basically my position earlier today. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after the examination-in-chief and after Mr. Zecevic has finished, my cross-examination will substantially be curtailed, so I don't think I would use more than half an hour. So I believe that we can finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will work on the assumption that Ms. Tabeau will be available for testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly. Your Honour, can I just mention in passing, though, just for perhaps after the break, that maybe the cross-examination estimates could be a little bit more realistic than they have been for the last few weeks. I mean, we really have, I mean, you know, from three hours down to 15 minutes is a really massive drop. And we can only organise for the witnesses to come on the basis of what we're told what will be cross-examination. So we have been running out of witnesses the last few weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber shares that concern and I trust that when we return after the summer break that the estimates with which we are provided would -- would be more in keeping with what is likely to happen, because everyone shares the concern about wasted court days. Yes, the usher can escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, on the 12th of June, you were taken from your home at around 3.00 p.m., and if I understood you correctly, on that same day, you were brought to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic, please proceed continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
