utterances.text: Since I interrupted you, I will share with counsel what I was just consulting with Judge Delvoie and then later with the legal officer sotto voce about, and that is the matter raised by Ms. Korner as to the rule about not being able to consult a witness who is part heard during an adjournment, and I was comparing the -- the general exception, as I understand it, to this rule in common law practice to a person who was an expert witness. And I appreciate that in this case, there is controversy as to whether she is an expert but the Chamber has nevertheless ruled, so I appreciate that the Defence is not ad idem with the Prosecution on this. So perhaps by tomorrow, if it is necessary for us to revisit this, we may have to look at the question as to whether this absolute prohibition would apply to a witness such as Ms. Tabeau. Because, of course, rules always have to be applied in a way that they make sense and that they facilitate rather than frustrate the process. So, as I said, we may return to this tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when on the 12th you arrived there, I think that you confirmed today again that at that point the commander of Keraterm was a certain Zivko Knezevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood your evidence correctly today and your testimony on page 897 of 21st of March, 2001, only after two or three days was the running of Keraterm taken over by Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking. Well, let's say five to six days. But it was a relatively short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This person, Zivko Knezevic, was also a retired policeman, and he retired before the war.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown P662.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a document that has been shown to you by the Prosecution. A while ago you had a look at this document, right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document please be pulled up a little bit because I need to show the witness the heading of the document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner it says "RSM Prijedor II." This is the War Police Station Prijedor II. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this document is entitled: "The list of police employees to be given special access passes to the Keraterm reception centre." And down at the bottom - if we can now pull it down, please - it is signed by this Zivko Knezevic, the station commander. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, it is handwritten here that, I think, took over 54 passes on the 25th of June, 1992. Milenko Popovic and his signature is below. Can you see that that is written there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that perfectly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, there are really 54 persons on this list; correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who this Milenko Popovic is? Are you familiar with that name?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean, he is not on the list. I reviewed the list. So you're not familiar with the name?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Neither the first or the last name, they don't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from whom this person had taken over these 54 passes? Do you have any idea who could -- who could they have been taken over from? Who issued them to him?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose the person who signed this document, and that is Zivko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know. But, sir, it says here the list of police employees to be given special access passes, and under number 1, Zivko Knezevic is listed. So he made the list and he placed himself under number 1 on it. And somebody else, a third person who is not in the list and neither you nor I know who is he, and that is the person by the name of Milenko Popovic, took over 54 passes on the 25th of June. It's not logical that he would take over the passes from Zivko Knezevic, right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it's logical or not. But if there were a typed-up date on the list that would state when it was made, then I would tell you that if I had been brought to the camp on the 12th of June, and if we take this period of five days, it's possible that Zivko Knezevic, as early as on the 15th, or on the 17th, was no longer the camp commander but was holding some other position. That is the logic of the questions that you have asked me, as far as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I agree with you. He signs himself here and says that he's the station commander. And we saw in the heading of the document that it says, "War Police Station Prijedor II." So, at the moment when he was making this list, Zivko Knezevic was the commander of that station. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: For me, Zivko Knezevic was a policeman whom I knew. I can describe how he looked physically. And, at the time, when I got to the Keraterm camp, he was the camp commander. At least three or four times during these several days, five or six days, I used to see him in the Keraterm camp. I really don't know. There could be three different Zivko Knezevics, but I know this one whom I used to see at the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony in the Sikirica case was that Dusko Sikirica, it is on page 897 on the 22nd of March, 2001, you said the following: "Sikirica came later, maybe 15 days after the day on which the camp was established. Before him, the retired -- a retired policeman was the commander and I think that his name was Zivko Knezevic." That was your testimony in the Sikirica case.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. The camp was established on the 31st of May. 15 days after the 31st of May is the 15th of June. Would two or three days mean anything in all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please. I'm not trying to do anything. I was just interested in one thing, and you had an impression that it was something else. It's not the way I wish to question you. I agree that lots of time has passed and I take into account the stress that you were under. There is no doubt that you got there on the 12th, and that three, four, or five days after that, Sikirica became the commander. I'm only interested, in connection with this document, as to whether you have any idea or knowledge from whom this Milenko Popovic could have taken over the 54 passes on the 25th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't. I'm sorry, but, no. I didn't know it; I couldn't know it; nor do I know it now. And even if I tried, I couldn't conclude anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is a fact, and you testified about that on page 977 on the 26th of March, 2001, that you had heard that behind the dormitories in Keraterm a unit of military police had stayed. Is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: We had some knowledge of that. Even that there was some sort of detention or, I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Islamovic. My name is Dragan Krgovic. On behalf of the Defence of Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, I will continue to question you and my questioning will last shorter than I announced, considering your testimony up until now, so maybe 20 minutes or half an hour, and I hope that we will finish your testimony today. Mr. Islamovic, when the Prosecutor asked you at the very beginning after reading the summary of your statement about Keraterm, there was something that remained unclear to me so I will ask you now whether I understood properly the essence of your testimony and what the Prosecutor read out. It has to do with the incident in Keraterm, the murder of prisoners, in front of dormitory number 3. As far as I understood your testimony and what the Prosecutor read out to you, a group of soldiers came to the camp, that is to say, Keraterm, and killed these men in dormitory number 3. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: You could put it that way. A group, that's a relative notion, a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you said that you heard that these were 100 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that they were soldiers who had come there from outside the camp. They were not in charge of guarding you but they came from someplace else. That was how I understood it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the guards who were standing guard, they came to the camp from outside, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question had to do with the adjudicated fact 1089 from the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Further, as far as I understood your testimony and the statement you gave earlier, at the Keraterm camp, at the time when you were detained there, all the inmates were men; correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps on one day, as far as I remember, two or three women passed through it, but either on that very day, or the next day, they were transferred to Omarska. So it was generally just men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question had to do with the adjudicated fact 893 and also 898.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamovic, my colleague Mr. Zecevic also asked you whether, in addition to your testimony in the Sikirica case, and your today's testimony before this Court, whether you gave several statements to the OTP. Generally speaking, I'm not interested in the statement, which I won't mention. Let me just ask you about the statements which you gave to the OTP. While reading your statements, I could see that some of the information that you provided to the OTP was your direct experience; correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And one part of your statement was based on the information which you collected or heard from other people while you were the president of the Association of Camp Inmates of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: President of the Camp Inmates Association of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Zecevic read out to you what you stated on the 24th of January, 2001, and you had the occasion to review it before coming to court today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you described the camp of Omarska -- I will read out to you how you described it. You said: "This camp was in full capacity, beginning on the 24th May until 5th of August, 1992. Most of the survivors were then transferred to the Trnopolje or Manjaca camps." Do you remember that that was what you said?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you described how the camp was run, in the last sentence you said this camp was run by the military even though there were some policemen who seemingly worked under the command of the army. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me say I do stand by that, though, at the moment, I really didn't think about this at all and I didn't find this important. In some of my statements when I said "the army," I also had in mind the police and the army and all the uniformed men who were on the other side, who were not inmates but were at the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The date of the statement is incorrect. There was a -- Mr. Krgovic I think said the 24th of March. Then there was an interpretation -- which said it was the 24th of -- that it was in January and then it was in March. In fact it's the 24th of August, 2001, that you're referring to. Just to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I said the 24th of August. Maybe it was a slip of the tongue but I think I did say the 24th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is unimportant. I remember the contents, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamovic, I'm sure you distinguish between the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You made that clear during the examination-in-chief. So taking into account your statements and testimonies, I just wanted to ask you if you stand by that and I wanted to read out a couple of sentences to you.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As you said during your testimony in the Sikirica case and in the statement, as for Keraterm, you said that the camp was in full capacity from the 30th of May until another date --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 5th of August and that it was under the control of the Serbian army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked about Trnopolje, which was open for a longer time, as you said, it was also under the control of the Serbian army, but of the three said camps, this one was the least notorious; correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Though some guards there also carried -- also wore all kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just another question that has to do with the certificate issued by the Red Cross. When you came to Trnopolje, the Red Cross -- that is to say, the address Andje Knezevic 18, is that the address where you would be staying after Trnopolje or was that the address of Trnopolje? I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's my home address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as I understood the certificate issued by the Red Cross, even though the copy is not very good, the Red Cross would accommodate you in your own house?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. According to the certificate, I spent the time between the 4th and the 7th of August at the Trnopolje camp, when we were received by the Red Cross after Keraterm, at the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So at the Trnopolje camp you were received by the Red Cross. And then on the 7th of August, you went home. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the certificate, it seems that the Red Cross received us but it wasn't like that. And it is correct that some inmates, if they had a Serb who could guarantee for them, as you can see on the back side of the certificate, then such an inmate could leave and return to his home in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Islamovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked some questions by my learned friend a little while ago about the statement you made to this Tribunal dated the 24th of August. I'm now referring to the questions posed by Mr. Zecevic earlier today. And he read out a portion of that statement to you. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the portion he read out said that -- it started by saying: "The Serbs had starting arresting the people of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity around 20th of May." Then it carried on and said: "The collection centres were the places where the arrested people were taken." Now do you recall in your statement directly before that paragraph you had listed the 41 detention facilities in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember that well. I wanted to react on that occasion. Maybe this is a good opportunity. One must make a distinction here between collection centres where people were kept for a period of two to five days and camps, death camps, such as Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. You were later asked about your -- some questions about whether you were -- had received a call-up before you were arrested. And I'm referring to page 40, where you said that you had received an assignment. Could you tell the Tribunal what your assignment was?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just help me? I'm not sure whether I understand what you're referring to by "assignment."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Certainly. You were asked a question by my learned friend which had a couple of issues in it, and I wanted you -- your answer was yes and that's why I wanted to clarify. I'll -- the portion of the question was -- the first part of the question was: "Once mobilisation is publicly declared, then the summons are not served personally but that meant that all those falling into this category were obliged to report to the unit, according to their assignment? "And you also had an assignment; is that correct?" And your answer was: "Yes." I just wanted to clarify whether your answer was -- your answer in the affirmative was to the first part or the second part of that question.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Your -- your statement is correct. The first part of the question, it was prescribed by the law, that all able-bodied men upon hearing of mobilisation must report to their military departments where their papers were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you personally receive an assignment?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Neither myself nor my brothers, for that fact, none of my neighbours, Muslims or Croats that I knew of, or that I knew at the time, did not get any such personal assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. You were also asked some questions about the document with the list of names by my learned friend and about the passes that were given to the individuals in relation to Keraterm camp. Did you actually see any guards carrying passes while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I either didn't have a chance of seeing the passes in question, or -- but in any case, the passes for us camp inmates were of no relevance. Anyone could have entered Keraterm camp at any point and do whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were also asked some questions about the women at Keraterm camp. Where were they housed?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they weren't housed at Keraterm. But I remember the name of a neighbour of mine who spent one night, only one night, either in dormitory number 1 or dormitory number 2. I think there must have been only two or three of them that spent just one night in Keraterm and then left to Omarska, together with the other -- with other inmates in -- I think it was in number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And just to clarify, this neighbour that you're speaking of is a woman?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, finally, sir, you were asked some questions by Mr. Krgovic just a few minutes ago about Trnopolje. And you said that the guards at Trnopolje while you were there wore all kinds of uniforms. Could you elaborate on that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: In my previous statements one can often see mention of either soldiers or people in uniform. Not even the soldiers wore uniforms that were all the same. Some wore JNA uniforms, olive-drab, in other words. Then others wore camouflage uniforms, grey-green uniforms with patches. And then there was a third type, blue police uniforms with light blue shirts. Police shirts, very conspicuous.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, and unless Your Honours have any questions, I seek to tender his 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. The --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 10400 -- 10401 will become Exhibit P1525.1; and 65 ter number 10402 will become Exhibit P1525.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I was reminding myself about the -- about that extra -- but, of course, that's not a part of the 92 ter package, the one that was marked for identification, the Red Cross document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Islamovic, you told us that the prison warden, Knezevic, was before the war a retired police officer and that he came back during these events as a reserve police officer, right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: How about Mr. Sikirica? What was he -- what was his position before the war, if you know; and what was he -- was he a police officer, a reserve police officer, while the prison warden?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can answer your question because I know it. My friend worked in Celpak factory. I believe he was not a policeman. Whether he was a reserve policeman, I don't know that, but he was an employee of Celpak factory. And I know that for sure that he was not an active policeman before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then do you know of any rape cases of female detainees in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: MENSUR ISLAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any rape cases in -- for Keraterm camp, but at a later stage, I heard that in Omarska there was quite a few rapes, that about 20 women were arrested and kept there, and I talked to them later on in Trnopolje, and later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Islamovic, for your testimony before the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. And we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we would resume this trial tomorrow morning. We're back in Courtroom III. Now, you had something before we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just simply this, Your Honours. The question obviously of whether we can speak to Ms. Tabeau, or anybody from the OTP, perhaps could we have the ruling on that before she begins her evidence so that we all know where we are. She's obviously -- she is a witness in other cases and therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment. Since we aren't rising immediately --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- I will ask the usher to escort the witness from the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, going back to the point that you raised, my recollection or understanding is -- even in the common law system is even with an expert, once he has started to testify, he is not allowed to discuss matters with counsel from the side that's calling him or, indeed, from the other side. Of course, exceptions can always be made in the interests of -- of keeping things moving smoothly. With Ms. Tabeau, as with other witnesses who Your Honours have heard who work here, I know she's certainly testifying in other cases and it may be that during the adjournment - I don't know - some of the other cases may want to speak to her about -- about matters. Now, again, that's a matter Your Honours may want to consider. But from this case, I think the only point is this: That if she's going to correct any of her figures once she's started, it may well be that - can I put it this way? - this is out of pure caution. She can simply put it down into -- into a statement. I just raise it as a matter of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was wondering, Ms. Korner, if any corrections have to be made, as you described it, why would you have to discuss it with Ms. Tabeau out of court?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, I have no idea. This is an abundance of caution. But I do know -- or it may be Your Honour wants to ask questions, but, in fact, I think she is going to be able to explain tomorrow why she wants to make the corrections, so that should in any event deal with it. And, secondly, Your Honours, in hopes -- in hopes, because there's a lot of work that needs to be done, we'll be filing probably tomorrow, so two days earlier -- no, one day earlier, a corrected list of witnesses. But we wondered if we can have an exchange, perhaps the decision on the other witnesses because of the work that needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which one --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The one where we said we would like to drop eight but replace it with five, and if that was possible before the adjournment we would be most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We are trying that one as well, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When I mentioned earlier about the professional witnesses -- and I was thinking out loud so my thoughts may not have been as clearly developed as they should have been, but I was thinking of the practical reality that the basis for the rule would -- must necessarily have been different historically from a witness as to the facts who could be influenced to -- by discussions with counsel to change his or her testimony than a pure -- let's take a person who is a fire-arms expert whose report would be his report, regardless of which side called him or whether he is called by the Bench and therefore there would be no -- the likelihood of being influenced would be remote. But as I said, we would have to devise a -- we'd come with a practical solution to the problem that you've identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As I said, it's pure -- I think it was just to safe-guard the potential position. Not so, indeed, so much for our case, but the question of whether counsel from other cases need to talk to her. We are hoping to have her back for cross-examination - Ms. Pidwell did it - but I think it's the second week after the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, counsel, we can think about it overnight and if counsel have further views, we would -- as you said, if we would -- if we have to formally rule on this to do so before the witness is sworn --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- and we do so tomorrow morning. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. And, Your Honours, I'm told that the second week after we're back she should be returning for cross-examination, on our estimates. That will give Mr. Zecevic lots of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.47 p.m.,
